author: A Robot
objectives: Identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order.
Distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions.
Explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to systemic versus pulmonary pressure requirements.
Describe the function of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow, and identify which valves separate which chambers or chamber-vessel pairs.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1: Exterior Orientation of the Heart
modules.description: An intact and a cutaway heart model appear side by side. Narration establishes anatomical orientation and explains why left/right labels are reversed from the viewer's perspective.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Orient the heart anatomically with the apex pointing down and to the left.
Understand that left and right refer to the patient's own orientation, not the viewer's.
Recognize the difference between the intact exterior view and a cutaway interior view.
instructions: Grab either heart model to rotate both together and view from any angle.
Use Next/Previous to move through the narration.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce the intact heart model alone and welcome the student, establishing the exterior view as the starting point.
clips.narration: Welcome to your exploration of the human heart. In front of you is a full-size model of the heart, oriented as it sits in the chest: the pointed apex angles down and toward the patient's left side.

clips.changeMeaning: Bring in the cutaway heart beside the intact one so students can compare exterior and interior at once.
clips.narration: Beside the intact heart is a cutaway view with the anterior wall removed. Through it you can see the four chambers, the dividing septum, and the four valves that the exterior surface hides.

clips.changeMeaning: Slowly rotate both hearts and reveal the orientation label to explain the reversed left/right convention.
clips.narration: As you rotate the models, notice we describe sides from the patient's perspective. What appears on your left is the patient's right side, and vice versa. This convention is standard in all clinical settings.

modules.description: A cutaway heart is toured structure by structure. Labels appear beside each chamber, valve, and vessel in a defined sequence, mapping interior structures to exterior landmarks.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Name the four chambers in order: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle.
Name the four valves and the chambers/vessels they separate.
Name the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Recognize the dual naming of the mitral/bicuspid valve.
instructions: Follow the highlighted structures with the narration.
Use Next/Previous to move through each structure.

clips.changeMeaning: Begin the tour at the chambers, highlighting the right atrium and showing its label.
clips.narration: We begin with the four chambers. The right atrium, upper right of the heart, receives deoxygenated blood returning from the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Move the highlight and label to the right ventricle to continue the chamber sequence.
clips.narration: Below it, the right ventricle pumps that deoxygenated blood toward the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Advance to the left atrium, switching to red labeling to distinguish oxygenated-side chambers.
clips.narration: On the patient's left, the left atrium receives oxygenated blood returning from the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the left ventricle, completing the chamber sequence.
clips.narration: The left ventricle, the heart's most muscular chamber, pumps oxygenated blood to the entire body.

clips.changeMeaning: Shift focus to the valves, starting with the tricuspid, and reset highlight color to the valve theme.
clips.narration: Now the four valves. The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and right ventricle, letting blood flow forward while preventing backflow.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the pulmonary valve to continue the valve sequence.
clips.narration: The pulmonary, or pulmonic, valve sits between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk leading to the lungs.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the mitral valve and note its dual name, an important clinical distinction.
clips.narration: The mitral valve, also called the bicuspid valve, sits between the left atrium and left ventricle. You will see both names used in clinical and anatomical settings.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the aortic valve to complete the valve sequence.
clips.narration: The aortic valve sits between the left ventricle and the aorta, the great artery carrying blood to the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Move to the great vessels, highlighting the superior and inferior vena cava on the intact-side landmarks.
clips.narration: Finally, the major vessels. The superior and inferior vena cava return deoxygenated blood from the upper and lower body into the right atrium.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the pulmonary arteries and veins, emphasizing their reversed oxygenation relative to systemic vessels.
clips.narration: The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs, while the pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood — the opposite of the usual artery-vein pattern.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the aorta to conclude the vessel tour.
clips.narration: And the aorta arches up from the left ventricle, delivering oxygenated blood to the whole body. That completes our structural tour.

modules.description: The cutaway heart fills with color-coded flowing blood — blue for deoxygenated, red for oxygenated — while the pulmonary and systemic circuits are labeled and highlighted in turn.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish deoxygenated (blue) from oxygenated (red) blood pathways.
Identify the pulmonary circuit and the systemic circuit as two distinct loops.
Explain that the right heart serves the lungs and the left heart serves the body.
instructions: Watch the continuous flow to see the steady-state pattern.
Use Next/Previous to isolate each circuit.

components.scriptDescription: Animates a looping particle-like stream of colored fluid along a defined path of waypoints to represent flowing blood. Inputs (settable in inspector): an ordered list of Transform waypoints defining the flow path, a flow speed in units per second (default 0.2), and a stream color. Output: continuously moves and recycles flow segments along the waypoint path, producing a visible directional current. Used to show steady-state circulation direction.

Animates a looping particle-like stream of colored fluid along a defined path of waypoints to represent flowing blood. Inputs (settable in inspector): an ordered list of Transform waypoints defining the flow path, a flow speed in units per second (default 0.2), and a stream color. Output: continuously moves and recycles flow segments along the waypoint path, producing a visible directional current.

clips.changeMeaning: Start both color-coded streams flowing to show the full steady-state dual circulation.
clips.narration: Now watch blood move through the heart. Blue marks deoxygenated blood on the right side; red marks oxygenated blood on the left. Both flow continuously in steady state.

components.text: Right heart -> lungs -> back to left heart

clips.changeMeaning: Isolate the pulmonary circuit by dimming the oxygenated stream and labeling the pulmonary loop.
clips.narration: The pulmonary circuit is the short loop: the right side of the heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, where it releases carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen.

components.text: Left heart -> whole body -> back to right heart

clips.changeMeaning: Isolate the systemic circuit by restoring the red stream, dimming the blue, and relabeling.
clips.narration: The systemic circuit is the long loop: the left side of the heart pumps oxygenated blood to the entire body, then it returns deoxygenated to the right side.

components.text: Pulmonary and systemic circuits run in series

clips.changeMeaning: Restore both streams to full color and summarize the central insight of the two loops working together.
clips.narration: Together the two circuits form one continuous system: right side to the lungs, left side to the body, endlessly cycling. Keep this dual organization in mind as we trace a single cell next.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4: Step-by-Step Red Blood Cell Trace
modules.description: A single red blood cell is followed step by step through the entire circulation, changing from blue to red at the lungs, with a label naming each structure it enters.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the complete path of blood through the heart in order.
Identify where in the circuit blood becomes oxygenated.
Reinforce the sequence of chambers, valves, and vessels.
instructions: Press Next to advance the cell one step along its path.
Use Previous to step back and replay any part of the trace.

clips.changeMeaning: Place the blue deoxygenated cell in the superior vena cava as the starting point of the trace.
clips.narration: Our journey begins with a deoxygenated red blood cell — shown blue — entering the heart through the superior vena cava.

clips.changeMeaning: Move the cell into the right atrium as the first chamber of the trace.
clips.narration: The cell flows into the right atrium, the first chamber, which collects blood returning from the body.

clips.changeMeaning: Advance the cell through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle as the atrium contracts.
clips.narration: The right atrium contracts, pushing the cell through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Push the cell through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk as the ventricle contracts.
clips.narration: The right ventricle contracts, driving the cell through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.

clips.changeMeaning: Route the cell out through the pulmonary arteries toward the lungs.
clips.narration: From the trunk, the cell travels through the pulmonary arteries toward the lungs — remember, these arteries carry deoxygenated blood.

clips.changeMeaning: At the lung capillaries the cell changes color from blue to red to show oxygen pickup.
clips.narration: In the lung capillaries the cell releases carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen. Watch it change from blue to red as it becomes oxygenated.

clips.changeMeaning: Return the now-red cell through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium.
clips.narration: The oxygenated cell returns through the pulmonary veins — veins carrying oxygen-rich blood — into the left atrium.

clips.changeMeaning: Advance the cell through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.
clips.narration: The left atrium contracts, pushing the cell through the mitral valve into the powerful left ventricle.

clips.changeMeaning: Eject the cell through the aortic valve into the aorta and out to the body.
clips.narration: The left ventricle contracts forcefully, sending the cell through the aortic valve into the aorta and out to the entire body.

clips.changeMeaning: Return the cell blue through systemic veins to the superior vena cava, closing the loop.
clips.narration: After delivering oxygen to the tissues, the cell turns blue again and returns through the systemic veins to the superior vena cava, completing the loop. Replay the trace anytime.

modules.description: Two horizontal cross-sections compare the thin right ventricular wall with the much thicker left ventricular wall, with scale markers confirming the roughly 3:1 ratio.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare the myocardial thickness of the right and left ventricles.
Relate wall thickness to the pressure required for pulmonary versus systemic circulation.
Confirm the approximate 3:1 thickness ratio using scale markers.
instructions: Grab a cross-section to rotate and compare the walls directly.
Use Next/Previous to step through the comparison.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the right ventricle cross-section and reveal its thin-wall label.
clips.narration: Here are two cross-sections cut at the same level through the ventricles. On the left, the right ventricle has a thin wall, only about three to five millimeters thick.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the left ventricle cross-section and reveal its thick-wall label for direct comparison.
clips.narration: On the right, the left ventricle's wall is far thicker — roughly ten to fifteen millimeters, about three times the right ventricle's thickness.

clips.changeMeaning: Rotate both cross-sections slowly and explain the functional pressure-based reason for the asymmetry.
clips.narration: Why the difference? The right ventricle only pumps blood a short distance to the low-pressure lungs. The left ventricle must generate much higher pressure to push blood through the entire body, so it needs far more muscle.

modules.moduleName: Scene 6: Valve Function and Backflow Prevention
modules.description: The four valves are examined in open and closed states, grouped into atrioventricular and semilunar valves, showing how they prevent backflow during the cardiac cycle.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish atrioventricular valves from semilunar valves.
Explain how each valve group prevents backflow.
Identify which valves are open and closed during ventricular contraction versus relaxation.
instructions: Step through the open and closed states of each valve.
Use Next/Previous to move through the cardiac phases.

components.text: AV valves: tricuspid & mitral. Semilunar valves: pulmonary & aortic.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduce the two valve categories, showing both AV and semilunar valves in a neutral state.
clips.narration: The heart has two kinds of valves. The atrioventricular valves — tricuspid and mitral — sit between atria and ventricles. The semilunar valves — pulmonary and aortic — sit between ventricles and their outflow arteries.

components.text: AV valves CLOSED, semilunar valves OPEN

clips.changeMeaning: Show ventricular contraction: AV valves closed, semilunar valves open, illustrating forward ejection.
clips.narration: During ventricular contraction, the atrioventricular valves snap closed to stop blood flowing back into the atria, while the semilunar valves open to let blood eject into the arteries.

components.text: AV valves OPEN, semilunar valves CLOSED

clips.changeMeaning: Show ventricular relaxation: AV valves open, semilunar valves closed, the reverse configuration.
clips.narration: During ventricular relaxation, the reverse happens: the semilunar valves close to stop blood falling back into the ventricles, while the atrioventricular valves open to let the ventricles refill.

components.text: Valves open and close in coordination to keep blood moving forward.

clips.changeMeaning: Summarize how coordinated valve timing enforces one-way flow through the whole cardiac cycle.
clips.narration: This alternating rhythm ensures blood always moves forward and never backward. If a valve fails to seal, blood leaks back — the basis of many valvular heart conditions you'll study clinically.

modules.description: The cutaway heart appears without labels. A structure is highlighted and the student selects its correct name from candidate options, cycling through chambers, valves, and vessels.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recall and identify heart structures without label prompts.
Reinforce the names of chambers, valves, and vessels.
Self-assess structural knowledge before the flow quiz.
instructions: A structure will be highlighted; select the correct name.
Use Next/Previous to move through the quiz items.

clips.changeMeaning: Present the first quiz item: highlight the right atrium with three chamber options to choose from.
clips.narration: Let's test your identification. Which structure is highlighted here? Select the correct name from the options below.

clips.changeMeaning: Confirm the correct answer and present the second item highlighting the mitral valve with valve options.
clips.narration: Correct — that's the right atrium. Now, which valve is highlighted between the left atrium and left ventricle?

clips.changeMeaning: Confirm the valve answer and present a vessel item highlighting the aorta with vessel options.
clips.narration: Correct — the mitral valve, also called the bicuspid. Last one: which great vessel is highlighted leaving the left ventricle?

clips.changeMeaning: Confirm the final answer and wrap up the structure quiz, inviting replay for reinforcement.
clips.narration: Correct — that's the aorta. Well done. You can replay this quiz to reinforce your identification of every structure.

modules.description: Given a starting position in the circulation, the student identifies the next structure in the path, stepping through the full pulmonary and systemic circuit and distinguishing arteries from veins.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Recall the correct sequence of structures in circulation.
Distinguish pulmonary arteries (deoxygenated) from pulmonary veins (oxygenated).
Self-assess mastery of the full blood flow path.
instructions: Read the starting position and choose the next structure in the path.
Use Next/Previous to step through the flow quiz.

components.text: What comes next in the path?
Blood just entered the RIGHT ATRIUM. What is next?

clips.changeMeaning: Present the first flow item starting at the right atrium, asking what structure comes next.
clips.narration: Now let's trace the path. A unit of blood has just entered the right atrium. Which structure does it pass through next?

components.text: Leaving the RIGHT VENTRICLE toward the lungs. Which vessel?

clips.changeMeaning: Confirm the answer, advance the cell, and pose the tricky pulmonary artery vs vein distinction.
clips.narration: Correct — the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. Here's a tricky one: after the right ventricle and pulmonary valve, blood heads to the lungs. Does it travel through pulmonary arteries or pulmonary veins?

components.text: Correct: Pulmonary Arteries carry DEOXYGENATED blood
Oxygenated blood returns via pulmonary veins to which chamber?

clips.changeMeaning: Confirm the artery answer, move the cell to the lungs turning red, and quiz the return to the left atrium.
clips.narration: Correct — pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs, the opposite of the systemic pattern. After oxygenation, which structure receives the blood returning from the lungs?

clips.changeMeaning: Confirm the final answer and complete the flow quiz, inviting replay.
clips.narration: Correct — the left atrium. You've traced the full circuit and mastered the artery-versus-vein distinction. Replay anytime to lock it in.

modules.description: A summary screen lists the five concept areas covered in the lab, each highlighted in turn as the narration reviews it, with the heart model rotating gently in the background.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Consolidate the five core concept areas of the lab.
Review the relationship between structure and function in the heart.
Prepare students to apply the concepts in assessment and clinical contexts.
instructions: Review each concept area as it is highlighted.
Use Next/Previous to move through the recap.

components.text: 3. Path of blood through the full circuit
4. Wall thickness asymmetry: left vs right ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight concept one and review the structural inventory of chambers, valves, and vessels.
clips.narration: Let's review. First, you built a structural inventory: four chambers, four valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.

clips.changeMeaning: Dim concept one, highlight concept two, and review the dual-circuit organization.
clips.narration: Second, you saw the dual-circuit organization: the right heart drives the pulmonary circuit to the lungs, the left heart drives the systemic circuit to the body.

components.text: 3. Path of blood through the full circuit

clips.changeMeaning: Dim concept two, highlight concept three, and review the traced path of blood.
clips.narration: Third, you traced a unit of blood through the entire circuit, from the vena cavae all the way around and back.

components.text: 3. Path of blood through the full circuit
4. Wall thickness asymmetry: left vs right ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: Dim concept three, highlight concept four, and review the wall thickness asymmetry.
clips.narration: Fourth, you compared ventricular walls and learned why the left ventricle is roughly three times thicker than the right — it pumps against much higher systemic pressure.

components.text: 4. Wall thickness asymmetry: left vs right ventricle

clips.changeMeaning: Dim concept four, highlight concept five, and close the lab with the valve-function review.
clips.narration: And fifth, you saw how the atrioventricular and semilunar valves open and close in coordination to keep blood flowing forward. Great work — you now understand both the structure and the function of the human heart.
